canonical_topic: Single-technology extreme case: marginal pricing eliminates profit and threatens new investment
definition: In the extreme case where a grid's generators all use similar technology (fully flat stack), marginal pricing sets everyone's clearing price near their common marginal cost, leaving no margin for anyone — which is a problem because new generation requires large upfront capital that must be recovered from operating profits.
core_idea: A fully flat stack under marginal pricing removes the profit that steep-stack marginal pricing normally provides; since new power plants need large initial investment recouped over time, a market with no sustained margin makes it hard for developers to attract financing, since lenders need assurance of a steady profit stream to be repaid.
key_points: If all generators share similar marginal cost, marginal-price clearing yields near-zero profit for everyone.
Building new generation requires large upfront capital investment.
Lenders financing new plants need confidence in a steady profit stream to recover their loans.
A structurally flat, no-margin market therefore threatens the economics of new generation investment.
relationships: Extreme endpoint of the flat-stack marginal pricing problem described above.
trading_implications: Markets trending toward a flat generation stack may need capacity payments or other non-energy revenue mechanisms to keep new investment financeable, since energy-only marginal pricing alone may not support debt service.
caveats: Low or converging marginal costs across generators (often seen as good for consumers) can simultaneously be a red flag for long-term resource adequacy, since it undermines the investment case for new capacity.
